title: What does Git store when a file changes?
answer: Git writes only the objects whose bytes are new, and names unchanged content again by its id

checks.question: Adding world.txt leaves hello’s content unchanged. Why does the tree still need a new id when hello’s blob does not?
checks.answer: The tree’s bytes gain an entry for world.txt, so its content changes and gets a new id. Hello’s bytes stay unchanged, so the new tree can name the existing hello blob.

checks.question: If the second commit edits hello.txt to “hello again” instead, which ids change, and what happens to commit one’s objects?
checks.answer: The blob’s, the tree’s and the commit’s: each object holds the id of the one below it. Commit one’s blob, tree and commit stay in the store unchanged, reachable through commit two’s parent line.

checks.question: If main moves back to commit one, must Git change either commit’s content objects?
checks.answer: No. Moving main changes a reference, not the immutable objects it names. It selects a different existing snapshot without rewriting its blobs, tree or commit.

steps.title: Git hashes 13 bytes to name this blob
steps.line: a second commit adds world.txt. Does Git store these bytes again?
steps.caption: hello.txt contains hello followed by a newline. Git hashes its type-and-length header together with those content bytes; the resulting id names a blob. The blob stores content independently of the file name. What must be written when the next commit changes the file collection?
steps.picture: The content bytes "hello\n", one cell each with its hex value; The header bytes “blob 6” and a zero byte, in front of the content; An arrow labelled SHA-1 from the bytes to their id; The blob id ce013625030ba8dba906f756967f9e9ca394464a, its first seven digits highlighted; A brace under the first seven digits, ce01362: the name later pictures give the blob.

steps.title: A tree gives those bytes a name
steps.line: The name hello.txt is in the tree entry, not in the blob.
steps.caption: A tree associates the name hello.txt and its mode with the blob’s id. The same content object can therefore be named by different trees without copying it. Hashing the tree’s own bytes gives that collection of names and references an id too.

steps.title: A commit names a tree; a branch names a commit
steps.line: main → commit → tree → blob: each holds the next one’s id.
steps.caption: The branch main holds a commit’s id, and that commit names a tree. Following the references reaches the snapshot’s file names and contents. The commit can describe a whole snapshot by naming reusable objects instead of embedding every file’s bytes.

steps.title: Answer: no. Tree two names blob ce01362 again
steps.line: 3 new objects: world’s blob, tree two and commit two.
steps.caption: Git writes only the objects whose bytes are new, and names unchanged content again by its id. The new tree adds world.txt while naming hello’s original blob again. It needs a new tree, world’s blob and a new commit, but the two snapshots share hello’s unchanged content.

steps.title: Moving main to commit two changes one reference
steps.line: refs/heads/main now holds commit two’s id; no object is copied.
steps.caption: main now names commit two. Moving this reference does not copy the objects it reaches, and the parent link keeps commit one reachable. The content objects remain immutable while the branch name moves. This is the logical object model; compression of those objects on disk is a separate question.

steps.title: Commit two’s id depends on every object it reaches
steps.line: 7 of 80 digits match in place, about the 5 chance gives.
steps.caption: The tree and parent ids are part of the commit’s bytes. A changed reference therefore changes the object being hashed, even if much of the surrounding text stays the same. The matching hex digits are chance agreements, not a measure of how similar the file contents are.

steps.title: Answer: 3 new objects, a blob, a tree and a commit
steps.line: Changed bytes change every id above them.
steps.caption: Git writes only the objects whose bytes are new, and names unchanged content again by its id. Editing hello changes its blob’s bytes and id. That id changes the tree’s bytes, and the changed tree id changes the commit. The old objects remain intact; the new commit’s parent reference leads back to the earlier history.
